title: Near consequences bind as faith articles; remote ones are only theological opinions
source_text: XXIII. Quod spectat autem ad doctrinam quae ex Scriptura hauritur, & in scholis proponi solet, vel consistit in iis quae in Scriptura sacra reperiuntur diserte & expresse posita, aut saltem quae ex iis per consequentias proximas & evidentes deducuntur: cujus generis ea esse debent, quae tanquam articuli, & capita fidei credenda Christiano populo proponuntur, cum nota haereseos in illos qui contraria docent. Vel in iis quae quidem ex Scriptura recte & sane deducuntur, sed tamen non ita clare, & evidenter, & per consequentias magis subtiles & remotas: quod genus proprie non sunt articuli fidei, sed veritates, aut opiniones tantum Theologicae, quarum contrarium gravius appellari non debet, quam error, non vero nomine haereseos notari. Quemadmodum Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae ea tantum esse de fide statuunt, quae sunt a Conciliis suis perspicue & expresse definita, non vero quaecunque nectendo consequentias de consequentis ex iis sese recte colligere posse putant. Ideoque distinguunt inter fidei dogmata, & Theologorum suorum placita, atque sententias, prioribus haeresin, posterioribus errorem opponentes.
pass_a_gloss: But as for the doctrine which is drawn from Scripture and is wont to be set forth in the schools, it either consists in those things which are found in sacred Scripture placed expressly and distinctly, or at least which are deduced from them by nearest and evident consequences: of which kind those things ought to be which are proposed to the Christian people to be believed as articles and heads of faith, with the mark of heresy against those who teach the contrary. Or in those things which indeed are rightly and soundly deduced from Scripture, but yet not so clearly and evidently, and by more subtle and remote consequences: which kind properly are not articles of faith, but truths, or only Theological opinions, whose contrary ought not to be called by a graver name than error, and not to be branded with the name of heresy. Just as the Doctors of the Roman Church state that those things only are of faith which have been clearly and expressly defined by their Councils, not whatever they think they can rightly gather from them by linking consequences upon consequences. And therefore they distinguish between dogmas of faith and the opinions and sentences of their Theologians, opposing heresy to the former and error to the latter.
pass_b_english: Doctrine drawn from Scripture and taught in the schools is of two kinds.

First: what Scripture states expressly, or what follows by nearest, evident consequences. Those should be proposed to the church as articles and heads of faith, with the mark of heresy for those who teach the opposite.

Second: what is rightly and soundly drawn from Scripture, yet not so clearly, and by subtler, more remote consequences. Those are not properly articles of faith, but theological truths or opinions. Their contrary should be called error — not heresy.

Rome's own doctors say only what their councils have clearly and expressly defined is de fide — not whatever they think they can weave by chaining consequence upon consequence. So they distinguish faith dogmas from their theologians' opinions: heresy against the first, error against the second.

choices.why: School placita vs de fide dogmata.
